targetReport.description: Madagascar's resources law for its three-tier Collectivités Territoriales Décentralisées (Communes, Régions, Provinces), verified via direct download (hosted on the electoral commission CENI's own site, mirroring the full official text). KEY FINDING — Art. 194, the Impôt Synthétique repartition formula: "La répartition du produit de l'impôt synthétique... se fait comme suit : - 50% au profit du budget de la Commune ; - 30% au profit du budget de la Région ; - 10% au profit du budget de la Province ; - 10% au profit du Fonds national de péréquation." Further shared-tax formulas: Art. 195 (hydrocarbon royalty): 40% Commune / 30% Région / 10% Province / 20% Fonds national de péréquation; Art. 206 (telecom-mast tax): 50% Communes / 30% Régions / 20% Provinces. Art. 198-204 list commune-exclusive local taxes (civil-protection/dangerous-animal tax, a 'taxe de résidence pour le développement' explicitly earmarked for Fokontany-level development financing, a water/electricity-subscriber tax).

targetReport.title: Lei n.° 1/2008, de 16 de Janeiro — Regime financeiro, orçamental e patrimonial das autarquias locais e o Sistema Tributário Autárquico
targetReport.description: Mozambique's municipal finance law, verified via a Wayback Machine capture (2011) of the originating Ministério da Administração Estatal PDF, which is now offline (mae.gov.mz unreachable) — same primary text, accessed via the earliest available archival mirror rather than a dead live host. KEY FINDING — Art. 43(2): "O montante do Fundo de Compensação Autárquica é objecto de uma dotação própria a inscrever no Orçamento do Estado e é constituído por 1,5% das receitas fiscais previstas no respectivo ano económico" [The Fundo de Compensação Autárquica (FCA) amount is set by its own appropriation in the State Budget and consists of 1.5% of the fiscal revenue projected for the relevant economic year]. Art. 43(3): the fund's proceeds are "de afectação livre pelas autarquias beneficiárias" [freely allocable by the recipient municipalities]. Art. 44's distribution formula: "FCAa = NHa/NHT x 75%FCA + Ata/ATT x 25%FCA" — each municipality's share is 75% weighted by its population share (Número de Habitantes) and 25% by its territorial-area share (Área Territorial). Art. 51 lists the municipal tax system: Imposto Pessoal Autárquico, Imposto Predial Autárquico (IPRA), Imposto Autárquico de Veículos, Imposto Autárquico de Sisa, Contribuição de Melhorias, plus fee-based (not tax-based) 'taxas por Licenças Concedidas e por Actividade Económica.'
targetReport.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument (still in force as of this round; not superseded by Lei 12/2023, which governs institutional structure rather than finance).

 Sobre o IPRA
 

 O Imposto Predial Autárquico (IPRA) é um tributo  municipal anual que incide sobre o valor patrimonial dos prédios urbanos situados no território do município, conforme estabelecido na Lei n.º 1/2008, de 16 de Janeiro. results.basis: RESOLVED 2026-08-09 (browser/websearch session, closing G.64.md cheap check 2). The Bank of Canada's own explainer states the mechanism: 'What's behind your mortgage rate' (bankofcanada.ca, May 27, 2020) -- 'These include the prime rate, which is used by the banks as a basis for pricing variable-rate mortgages.' Typed uses_data_from rather than calculated_from, matching this file's own boc-prime-rate -> boc-policy-rate precedent: the explainer describes a market convention (prime plus or minus a lender-set spread), not a formula stated by the published series' own methodology page, and the published aggregate is a volume-weighted average of what banks actually charged rather than a recalculation of prime itself.

targetReport.title: Chartered Bank Prime Lending Rate
targetReport.description: The rate Canadian chartered banks quote as the basis for variable-rate lending — mortgages, lines of credit, most consumer and small business borrowing. results.basis: Council Regulation (EC) No 479/2009, consolidated text of 01/09/2014, Article 1(1): 'For the purposes of the Protocol on the excessive deficit procedure and of this Regulation, the terms in paragraphs 2 to 6 are defined according to Regulation (EU) No 549/2013 of the European Parliament and the Council of 21 May 2013 on the European system of national and regional accounts in the European Union (hereinafter referred to as ESA 2010). The codes in brackets refer to ESA 2010.' The dependence is operative, not decorative: Article 1(2) defines 'Government' as 'the sector of general government (S.13)... as defined in ESA 2010', Article 1(3) defines 'Government deficit (surplus)' as 'the net borrowing (net lending) (B.9) of the sector of general government (S.13), as defined in ESA 2010', and Article 1(5) defines 'Government debt' by ESA 2010 categories 'currency and deposits (AF.2); debt securities (AF.3) and loans (AF.4)'. 'Are defined according to' is derivation language and is not on Research.1.md section 5a's watchlist. Direction: the EDP Regulation is the dependent, ESA 2010 the depended-on. Re-fetched and re-read from EUR-Lex 2026-08-07 after G.50.md Finding 4 recorded the site serving nothing; the outage was transient. Quoted with EUR-Lex's in-line amendment markers stripped — the unstripped Article 1(1) reads with the whole clause inside a M2 insertion marker, because the original 2009 text referred to ESA 95.

The codes in brackets refer to ESA 2010.

targetReport.title: European System of Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010)
targetReport.publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
targetReport.description: The EU's national accounts framework, enacted as Regulation (EU) No 549/2013. Article 1(2) sets out its two parts: 'a methodology (Annex A) on common standards, definitions, classifications and accounting rules that shall be used for compiling accounts and tables on comparable bases for the purposes of the Union' and 'a programme (Annex B) setting out the time limits by which Member States shall transmit to the Commission (Eurostat) the accounts and tables'. Unlike the international standards already in this corpus, ESA 2010 is a Regulation — member states do not adopt it by choice — which is why the EU branch was expected to produce supranational-to-national edges the Canada/US pair lacks. Annex B turned out to name tables and deadlines rather than publications; see the _dropped entries here and in eu-draft-budget.json.
targetReport.cadence_note: A generational standard, revised roughly once every fifteen to twenty years: ESA 1995 preceded it, and a further revision is already anticipated. releases_per_year matches sna-2008 (0.05) so the two read at the same pulse rate; see _open_questions.

results.basis: SOR/2007-303 s. 8(1)(y), the payroll-tax revenue base, makes SEPH a named term in a statutory formula: 'P is the gross dollar value, before deductions, of the payrolls of all employers in the province for the calendar year that ends in the fiscal year, as determined by Statistics Canada on the basis of its Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours, other than the payrolls of (i) employers not included in that survey, and (ii) employers in the following industry classifications, as defined by the North American Industry Classification System: (A) the elementary and secondary schools industry group, (B) the hospitals subsector, (C) the nursing and residential care facilities subsector, (D) the provincial and territorial public administration subsector, and (E) the local, municipal and regional public administration subsector'. `calculated_from` because P is a term in the formula, not a consideration — the same test that makes boc-bank-rate calculated_from the policy rate. Note the provision also carves out its own exclusions by NAICS classification, so the edge to `naics` is stated in the same sentence. SCOPE, stated because the section number alone overstates it: s. 8 sits in DIVISION 2 — Nova Scotia, and defines revenue base 'For the purpose of sections 3.71 to 3.9 of the Act', which are the Nova Scotia additional-equalization provisions. SEPH does NOT appear in the DIVISION 1 all-provinces revenue base at s. 5 — the phrase 'payrolls' occurs nowhere in ss. 1 through 8(1)(j), because the 2007 reform folded payroll taxes into the personal-income base. So this is the Equalization Program depending on SEPH through one division of the Regulations, not through the general formula.

targetReport.title: European System of Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010)
targetReport.publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
targetReport.description: The EU's national accounts framework, enacted as Regulation (EU) No 549/2013. Article 1(2) sets out its two parts: 'a methodology (Annex A) on common standards, definitions, classifications and accounting rules that shall be used for compiling accounts and tables on comparable bases for the purposes of the Union' and 'a programme (Annex B) setting out the time limits by which Member States shall transmit to the Commission (Eurostat) the accounts and tables'. Unlike the international standards already in this corpus, ESA 2010 is a Regulation — member states do not adopt it by choice — which is why the EU branch was expected to produce supranational-to-national edges the Canada/US pair lacks. Annex B turned out to name tables and deadlines rather than publications; see the _dropped entries here and in eu-draft-budget.json.
targetReport.cadence_note: A generational standard, revised roughly once every fifteen to twenty years: ESA 1995 preceded it, and a further revision is already anticipated. releases_per_year matches sna-2008 (0.05) so the two read at the same pulse rate; see _open_questions.

release_schedule.note: 2030 is Eurostat's stated aim, not a locked legal date — the ESA 2030 proposal is still in consultation.

targetReport.title: European Statistics Code of Practice
targetReport.publisher: European Statistical System Committee (published by Eurostat)
targetReport.description: The ESS's self-regulatory quality standard, adopted by the European Statistical System Committee and applying to Eurostat and the national statistical authorities. Eurostat's own page: 'The European Statistics Code of Practice (CoP) is the cornerstone of the quality framework and sets the standards for developing, producing and disseminating European statistics. It defines 16 key principles for the institutional environment under which the EU and national statistical authorities operate, as well as for the statistical processes and output . It also includes a set of 84 indicators for the best practices and standards for each of the 16 principles.' The current edition's own title page reads 'Adopted by the European Statistical System Committee 16th November 2017'. It names its own place in a three-part framework: 'The common quality framework of the European Statistical System is composed of the European Statistics Code of Practice, the Quality Assurance Framework of the European Statistical System and the general quality management principles'.
targetReport.cadence_note: Revised editions, not periodic issues. Eurostat's 'History of the CoP' table gives three dated events and nothing else: '24 February 2005 Adoption of the CoP by the Statistical Programme Committee | September 2011 Revision of the CoP based on the results of the 1st round of ESS peer reviews | November 2017 Revision of the CoP based on the results of the 2nd round of ESS peer reviews'. Two revisions across twelve years is roughly one every six; 0.17 is that observed interval, not a stated commitment. Same treatment as the versioned-standard nodes (esa-2010, sna-2008).

release_schedule.note: No fixed periodicity found. Eurostat's director publicly flagged (Nov 2025) that a revision is 'urgently' being prepared, but no date has been set.

targetReport.title: Single Integrated Metadata Structure (SIMS)
targetReport.publisher: Eurostat, endorsed by the European Statistical System Committee
targetReport.description: The ESS's single reporting structure for quality and reference metadata, formed by unifying the two earlier structures. Eurostat's own metadata-standards page: 'SIMS is the inventory and conceptual framework for all ESS quality and reference metadata concepts.' Its live status is stated in the present tense on Eurostat's quality-reporting page: 'The ESS quality reporting standard is the Single Integrated Metadata Structure (SIMS).' The two structures it absorbed remain visible as subsets rather than separate publications: 'the Euro-SDMX metadata structure (ESMS): the ESMS is a subset of SIMS' and 'the ESS standard quality report structure (ESQRS): the ESQRS is a subset of SIMS focusing on detailed quality concepts' - which is why neither is a node here.
targetReport.cadence_note: Versions, not issues. The EHQMR's lineage statement: 'the two standards - ESQRS and ESMS - were combined in the Single Integrated Metadata Structure (SIMS), which was published in 2013. Minor updates were made in 2015 and SIMS 2.0 was adopted by the European Statistical System Committee.' Eurostat's quality-reporting page additionally lists 'Single Integrated Metadata Structure Guidelines v2.0 (2019)'. Three dated points across 2013-2019; 0.2 is the observed rate, and no stated review interval was found.

release_schedule.note: SIMS is a metadata standard/conceptual framework endorsed by the European Statistical System Committee, not a periodic statistical release. It has been revised twice in its history: v1.0 (~2009) and v2.0 (November 2015, ESSC-endorsed). No Eurostat, CROS, or interoperable-europe.ec.europa.eu page states a review cycle, revision schedule, or next planned update. Commission Recommendation (EU) 2023/397 references SIMS concepts for reference metadata reporting but does not establish a periodic revision cadence. Given the absence of any calendar or stated rule, and only two revisions in ~15+ years with no announced next version, this is best classified as irregular rather than assigning a fabricated periodicity.

results.basis: ESS handbook for quality and metadata reports, s. 3.2.2 (p.25): 'The definitions and compilation methods for the QPIs are specified in the ESS Guidelines for the Implementation of the ESS Quality and Performance Indicators.' The Handbook takes the definitions and the compilation methods for the indicators it requires from the named document, which is methodology_depends_on rather than cites. Deliberately NOT built on the adjacent 'SIMS incorporates the 16 standard ESS Quality and Performance Indicators (QPIs)' sentence, which is a part_of statement about the indicator set and not an input claim about the document; see the caveat entry.
results.evidenceQuote: The definitions and compilation methods for the QPIs are specified in the ESS Guidelines for the Implementation of the ESS Quality and Performance Indicators.

targetReport.title: ESS Guidelines for the Implementation of the ESS Quality and Performance Indicators
targetReport.description: The document that defines the sixteen standard ESS Quality and Performance Indicators (QPIs) and states how each is computed. Its own title page reads 'ESS GUIDELINES FOR THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE ESS QUALITY AND PERFORMANCE INDICATORS (QPI)' and 'Version 1.4'. The ESS Handbook for Quality and Metadata Reports names it as the source of the definitions: 'The definitions and compilation methods for the QPIs are specified in the ESS Guidelines for the Implementation of the ESS Quality and Performance Indicators.' NOTE, and this is the reason the node is the Guidelines document and not 'the QPIs': the indicators themselves live inside SIMS and the ESQRS as sub-concepts ('SIMS incorporates the 16 standard ESS Quality and Performance Indicators (QPIs) within the sub-concepts (for user reports) and as sub-concepts of their own (for producer reports)'), which is the same part_of shape that keeps ESMS and ESQRS out of this slice. The indicator set is part of SIMS; the document that defines it is not.
targetReport.cadence_note: Versions, not issues, and the rate is a judgement between two readings that the document does not settle. Its own p.1: 'These indicators were reviewed by the Eurostat Expert Group on Quality Indicators in 2010 and then slightly updated by the Task Force on Quality Reporting in 2012-2013' - producing Version 1.4, which Eurostat's Tools and standards list dates as 'ESS Quality and Performance Indicators (2014)'. Read narrowly, that is two revision events across 2010-2014, roughly one every two years. Read across the observed lifetime, it is two revisions and then nothing at all for the twelve years to 2026. 0.13 is the lifetime reading (2 revisions / 16 years), chosen as the conservative one and the same treatment ess-quality-assurance-framework already carries; the narrow reading is recorded here rather than discarded. No stated review interval was found in the document or on Eurostat's quality-reporting page.

release_schedule.note: This is a methodological guidance document (defining the 18 ESS Quality and Performance Indicators), not a periodic statistical release. It has been revised occasionally, reproduced within the broader 'ESS Handbook for Quality Reports' / 'ESS Handbook for Quality and Metadata Reports' series: 2009 edition, 2014 edition (the version at the corpus's current URL), a 2020 edition (Feb 2020, KS-GQ-19-006), and a 're-edition 2021' (Dec 2021, KS-GQ-21-021). Gaps between editions are irregular (5 years, then 6 years, then ~1.75 years). The 2020 handbook states revisions are proposed via periodically-convened Task Forces of the Working Group on Quality in Statistics, with no fixed/stated cycle or calendar. No edition newer than the 2021 re-edition was found as of 2026-08-11.

targetReport.title: Productive Safety Net Programme Phase 5 (PSNP5) Design Document
targetReport.publisher: Government of Ethiopia (Ministry of Agriculture) with donor partners
targetReport.description: Ethiopia's flagship rural safety-net programme, now in its fifth phase. VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session (direct fetch of the Design Document, hosted via the EU's capacity4dev platform): Text Box 5 states 'Adequacy of transfers will be addressed through annual adjustments to the wage rate in line with consumer price index (CPI) to protect its real value.' Independently corroborated from the funding side (Grok's round): a World Bank results-framework indicator for the programme reads 'Increase in average wage rate relative to the annual general CPI increase, for cash transfers beneficiaries' -- two different documents, government-authored and donor-authored, both treating the wage-CPI link as real. This is a real-terms CPI-anchoring principle, similar in shape to Egypt's statutory pension floor, though PSNP5's own instrument is a programme design document rather than primary legislation -- a different evidentiary tier worth being precise about. The docx's more specific wheat-equivalency figures (15kg/16.95kg per month) remain unconfirmed -- see _open_questions.
targetReport.cadence_note: Wage-rate review conducted annually, before June each year per the docx's own quote (not independently re-confirmed this session against the fetched content).

release_schedule.note: The PSNP5 Design Document is a one-off program design document produced by the Ethiopian Ministry of Agriculture (with donor partners including the EU and World Bank) for the fifth phase of the Productive Safety Net Programme, covering 2021-2025 (source: capacity4dev.europa.eu library entry 'Ethiopia Productive Safety Net Programme 2021-2025 Phase V Design Document, FDRE Ministry of Agriculture, 2021'). It is not a recurring/periodical publication — it was produced once at the start of Phase 5. The programme has since moved into a new phase, PSNP6, which was approved/launched around March 2026 (World Bank press release, worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2026/03/03/ethiopia-a-new-phase-of-support-for-safety-nets...; World Bank project documents for P511478 'Productive Safety Net Program 6'). Since PSNP5 is already superseded by PSNP6's own separate design/project documents, no further release of 'the PSNP5 Design Document' specifically is expected. Historical PSNP phase lengths have also been irregular (PSNP2 ~2007-2009, PSNP3 2010-2014, PSNP4 2015-2020, PSNP5 2021-2025), so even treating this as a 'per-phase' publication would not yield a fixed/computable cadence.

results.window:
The SEASN project, approved in November 2020, is an Investment Project
    Financing (IPF) with Performance Based Conditions (PBCs). The SEASN project supports the Government of Ethiopia
    (GoE) flagship Productive Safety Net Programme Phase Five (PSNP 5) which provides a predictable safety net for
    Ethiopia’s poorest populations in the form of cash or food transfers to 7.9 million people either in return for
    participation in public works or unconditionally to households without adults who are work-able. PSNP 5 is facing a
    severe financing crisis caused by persistent extreme climate events (droughts) and conflict that have increased
    social protection needs, combined with a reduction in development partner and government financing and
    escalating costs due to the high rates of inflation.

targetReport.title: European System of Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010)
targetReport.publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
targetReport.description: The EU's national accounts framework, enacted as Regulation (EU) No 549/2013. Article 1(2) sets out its two parts: 'a methodology (Annex A) on common standards, definitions, classifications and accounting rules that shall be used for compiling accounts and tables on comparable bases for the purposes of the Union' and 'a programme (Annex B) setting out the time limits by which Member States shall transmit to the Commission (Eurostat) the accounts and tables'. Unlike the international standards already in this corpus, ESA 2010 is a Regulation — member states do not adopt it by choice — which is why the EU branch was expected to produce supranational-to-national edges the Canada/US pair lacks. Annex B turned out to name tables and deadlines rather than publications; see the _dropped entries here and in eu-draft-budget.json.
targetReport.cadence_note: A generational standard, revised roughly once every fifteen to twenty years: ESA 1995 preceded it, and a further revision is already anticipated. releases_per_year matches sna-2008 (0.05) so the two read at the same pulse rate; see _open_questions.

targetReport.title: Supply, Use and Input-Output Tables (SUIOTs)
targetReport.description: Matrices balancing supply and use of products across the economy to compile a single coherent GDP estimate. Eurostat's own page: 'Supply, use and input-output tables (SUIOTs) are matrices that provide a detailed picture of how goods and services are supplied and used in an economy.' Every country compiles its own SUIOTs and delivers them to Eurostat, which compiles the consolidated EU/euro-area version. Governed by the ESA 2010 transmission programme (Regulation (EU) No 549/2013, amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/734).
targetReport.cadence_note: Live-verified on Eurostat's own naio_10_n metadata page. Core tables (supply table, use table) are annual, delivered at t+36 months under the ESA 2010 transmission programme; a further set (use table at basic prices, margin tables, input-output tables) is delivered every 5 years (years ending in 0 or 5). releases_per_year reflects the annual core product.

entries.covers: Annual update of Supply and Use tables for the EU and euro area (FIGARO-based aggregate)

release_schedule.note: Eurostat does not publish a fixed-date release calendar entry for SUIOTs. National-level tables (naio_10_n) are published on a rolling/continuous basis throughout the year as individual countries transmit validated data (legal deadline: within 36 months after the end of the reference year, per the ESA 2010 transmission programme). The EU/euro-area consolidated aggregate (FIGARO-based), covered by the Statistics Explained article 'Supply and use tables for the European Union and the euro area', is updated once a year in autumn; the article itself states 'Data extracted: October 2025. Planned article update: October 2026', which is the closest thing to a stated next-release date and matches the corpus's releases_per_year=1.

results.window: Preserving confidentiality is an issue for supply and use tables received from EU Member States, countries of the European Free Trade Agreement (EFTA), and EU candidate countries. Any data flagged as confidential enter the compilation of FIGARO tables and are fully retained in the internal reference system used for balancing and consistency checks. However, in the final dissemination step, confidential data are replaced by adjusted values obtained through a controlled tabular adjustment procedure combined with pre-masking of key aggregates.

Because the December adoption date is only observed (not stated as a fixed rule) and Eurostat's grants page did not expose a full year-by-year archive to WebFetch (JS-rendered 'Previous financing decisions' section), this is classified as observed-pattern rather than published-calendar or stated-rule.

results.basis: The CRA page opens: 'Each year, certain personal income tax and benefit amounts are indexed to inflation using the Consumer Price Index data as reported by Statistics Canada.' The statutory mechanism is Income Tax Act s. 117.1(1)(b)(ii), which sets the adjustment factor as (A/B) - 1 where 'A is the Consumer Price Index for the 12 month period that ended on September 30 next before that year, and B is the Consumer Price Index for the 12 month period immediately preceding'; s. 117.1(4) defines that index as 'the Consumer Price Index for Canada, as published by Statistics Canada under the authority of the Statistics Act' averaged over the twelve months of the period. The published indexation factors (2.0% for 2026, 2.7% for 2025, 4.7% for 2024, 6.3% for 2023) are the direct output and drive every indexed bracket threshold and credit amount in the CRA table. See also https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/I-3.3/section-117.1.html

targetReport.title: Employment Insurance Maximum Insurable Earnings (MIE)
targetReport.publisher: Canada Employment Insurance Commission / Employment and Social Development Canada
targetReport.description: The annual ceiling on earnings on which EI premiums are payable and on which EI benefits are calculated, announced each September for the following year. It is set by a formula in section 4 of the Employment Insurance Act driven by Statistics Canada's Average Weekly Earnings of the Industrial Aggregate, and is rounded down to the nearest $100. The 2026 MIE is $68,900, up from $65,700 in 2025.

release_schedule.rule: Employment Insurance Act, s.4: the maximum yearly insurable earnings for a year is 52 times the average, for the 12-month period ending April 30 of the year immediately before that year, of the Average Weekly Earnings of the Industrial Aggregate in Canada (as published by Statistics Canada) for each month in that period, adjusted by the year-over-year percentage change in that average, and rounded down to the nearest multiple of $100. The resulting amount takes effect January 1 of that year, and CEIC/ESDC publishes an updated 'Maximum Insurable Earnings' notice each year (historically via a September/October news release; more recently as an updated canada.ca notice page, e.g. the 2026 notice was published 2025-10-31) ahead of the January 1 effective date.

 The number of weeks for which you may receive benefits doesn’t change if you move to another region after your benefit period begins. How we calculate your weekly benefit amount

 The amount of weekly benefits is calculated as follows:

 
 we calculate your total insurable earnings for the required number of best weeks (the weeks that you earned the most money, including insurable tips and commissions) based on the information you provide or your record of employment (ROE)

 we determine the divisor (number of best weeks) that corresponds to your regional rate of unemployment

 we divide your total insurable earnings for your best weeks by your required number of best weeks

 we then multiply the result by 55% to obtain the amount of your weekly benefits

 
 In regions of Canada with the highest rates of unemployment, we’ll calculate using the best 14 weeks. In regions of Canada with the lowest rates of unemployment, we’ll use the best 22 weeks.

targetReport.title: Consumer Price Index (Ghana Statistical Service)
targetReport.description: VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session via GSS's own CPI Technical Methodology Manual (v5, published October 2020) and its own recent press releases. The v5 manual: 'GSS uses 13 out of the 15 Divisions as distinguished by the COICOP manual', organised into '44 Groups, 98 Classes, 156 Subclasses, and 307 Item-level observations', and 'to order products into these different categories, GSS uses the United Nations Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (COICOP) 2018 manual.' Elementary aggregates: 'GSS uses the unweighted Jevons Index... the geometric mean of price relatives.' The v5 manual describes the then-current series on 'the whole year of 2018 as the price reference period' with 'weights based on the Ghana Living Standard Surveys 7 (GLSS7) from 2016/2017', and credits input from 'Statistics Denmark, and the International Monetary Fund (IMF)' plus ILO CPI-manual guidance. GSS has since rebased: the September 2025 press release (published 1 October 2025) states 'the price reference period has been updated to 2021 (2021=100)' with the weight reference period still 2017 -- confirmed independently, distinct from and more current than the v5 manual's own 2018=100 description. The rebase's own dedicated methodology note (as opposed to a press-release mention) was not located this session.

release_schedule.note: GSS publishes CPI/inflation monthly, consistently in 'Week 1' (occasionally week 2) of the month following the reference month. Observed 2026 releases: May 2026 CPI released ~June 4, 2026; June 2026 CPI released July 1, 2026; July 2026 CPI released Aug 6-7, 2026 (inflation 4.6%). GSS's own 2025 Statistical Product Release Calendar PDF confirms CPI is scheduled in Week 1 (or Week 2) of each month, but states the calendar 'will be updated quarterly' and no 2026 edition with exact dates was found online, so the September 2026 (for August 2026 data) date is inferred from the pattern rather than a published calendar entry.

targetReport.title: Ley Fundamental de Guinea Ecuatorial (Constitución)
targetReport.publisher: República de Guinea Ecuatorial (official constitutional text, hosted by FAOLEX)
targetReport.description: Equatorial Guinea's constitution. Artículo 3, apartados 4-5: "4. Se divide para los fines administrativos y económicos en Regiones, Provincias, Distritos y Municipios. 5. La ley determina los límites y las denominaciones de las regiones, provincias, distritos y municipios." Título Cuarto, "De las Corporaciones Locales," Artículo 131: "Las Corporaciones Locales son instituciones con personalidad jurídica propia, encargadas del gobierno y administración de las regiones, provincias, distritos y municipios. Promueven los planes y programas de desarrollo económico y social de sus respectivos territorios de acuerdo a la ley." Artículo 132.2: "La ley determina las competencias, el funcionamiento, la jurisdicción y la composición de las Corporaciones Locales." The Constitution itself establishes Municipios as one of four administrative/economic-division tiers and gives Corporaciones Locales legal personality, but explicitly delegates all finance/competency detail to ordinary law rather than stating a mechanism itself — the implementing law is Ley Número 1/2003 (see gq-ley-1-2003-administracion-local). Independently downloaded and text-extracted via pdftotext, not AI-summarized. Equatorial Guinea's official BOE portal (boe.gob.gq) could not be reached this round (503 Service Unavailable) to cross-verify against a more-authoritative host; the FAOLEX copy was used and is treated as reliable.

targetReport.title: Canadian and International Registration Manual
targetReport.description: A recurring commercial reference manual of vehicle registration and licence fee schedules by jurisdiction, published by R.L. Polk & Co. of Detroit. SOR/2007-303 names it verbatim at s. 8(1)(i) as the source of the licence-fee data behind the weighted average licence fee in the Nova Scotia division's motor vehicle licensing revenue base — the third commercial publication found inside a government funding formula, after J.D. Power in the US CPI and ICE Brent in Alberta's bitumen valuation.
targetReport.cadence_note: Historically issued as a recurring multi-volume manual. R.L. Polk & Co. was acquired by IHS in 2013 (now S&P Global Mobility) and no live publisher landing page for the manual could be found in 2026; the URL is a bibliographic record. The regulation continues to name it as the operative source, and the statutory citation, not the publisher's marketing page, is the evidence for the edge.

World Data Corp's press release (PRNewswire, Feb 16 2016) states the '2016 Motor Vehicle Registration Manuals Volumes I, II and III' were 'Released in mid-January [2016]', comparing page-count revisions against the 2015 edition -- indicating a recurring annual (mid-January) release cycle for the whole three-volume set. A dealer-facing 'World Data Corp (Polk Book) Quick Reference Guide' dated March 2025 confirms the product line (still informally called the 'Polk Book') was still active in 2025. No dated release calendar or exact-day rule was found, only this observed annual mid-January cadence, so this is marked observed-pattern rather than published-calendar or stated-rule. The corpus's existing releases_per_year=1 is consistent with this.

Alberta's share of Canada's total population continues to rise, which in turn increases Alberta's revenue share of the major federal transfers.' Canada Health Transfer appears as its own named revenue line ($6,633 million in 2026-27), and the forecast update attributes 'a combined $96 million increase in the Canada Health Transfer (CHT) and Canada Social Transfer (CST) due to a prior year adjustment and an upward revision of Alberta's provincial share of the national population in 2025.'

targetReport.title: Canada Health Transfer
targetReport.description: The largest major federal transfer to provinces and territories, providing federal cash support for health care and backing the criteria of the Canada Health Act. The national cash contribution is set in statute at section 24.1 of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act and escalates each year by a three-year moving average of nominal GDP growth subject to a 3 per cent floor; the national amount is then divided among provinces on an equal per capita basis under section 24.21. Finance Canada publishes provincial and territorial entitlement amounts each year before the start of the fiscal year.
targetReport.cadence_note: The escalator must be determined by the Minister of Finance not later than three months before the beginning of the fiscal year, i.e. by the end of December for the fiscal year starting the following April 1. Entitlements are re-estimated several times during and after the year under the CHT/CST Regulations, but there is one authoritative annual determination.

release_schedule.note: Finance Canada does not publish a formal release calendar or statutory publication deadline for CHT allocation announcements. However, a consistent annual pattern exists: the Minister/Deputy PM issues a news release in mid-to-late December each year announcing preliminary major federal transfer amounts (including CHT) for the fiscal year beginning the following April. Confirmed instances: Dec 2021 (for 2022-23), Dec 2022 (for 2023-24), Dec 15 2023 (for 2024-25), Dec 23 2024 (for 2025-26), and the major-federal-transfers.html table was updated Dec 11 2025 showing 2026-27 amounts (consistent with a Dec 2025 announcement). Separately, 'final' (as opposed to preliminary) CHT amounts for a fiscal year are determined about 6 months after that fiscal year ends (e.g., final 2025-26 amounts determined September 2026), per the same page's note, but this appears to be a data-finalization step rather than a public announcement event.

release_schedule.note: No release calendar or stated periodicity exists. The Manual has been issued only three times: 1989 (ILO, 'Consumer Price Indices: An ILO Manual'), 2004 ('Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice'), and 2020 ('Consumer Price Index Manual: Concepts and Methods'), each ~15-16 years apart. The IMF's own page for this report is titled 'Update of the Consumer Price Index Manual' and explains the 2020 edition was produced because 'methods and best practices have continued to evolve' since 2004, following requests from the 2014 UNECE-ILO CPI Experts Meeting -- i.e., updates are triggered by inter-agency expert consensus, not a fixed schedule. No next-edition date or working-group timeline is published. This is consistent with the corpus's very low releases_per_year (0.06, i.e. roughly once per 16 years).

Data from the Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours are used for many service industries.' The same sentence is the basis for the already-existing edge to statcan-seph, so `uses_data_from` follows that precedent. Corroborated independently by the programme's own source table, which names 'Monthly Survey of Manufacturing, Record no. 2101' in the gross-output rows for manufacturing industries — the same table and the same rows that produced the IPPI edge in V0.11.

targetReport.title: Monthly Survey of Manufacturing (MSM)
targetReport.description: Monthly survey of Canadian manufacturing sales, inventories, unfilled orders and capacity utilisation, IMDB record 2101. Named as an indicator source by the monthly GDP-by-industry programme for most manufacturing industries, and named alongside the IPPI in the deflation rows of that programme's source table. The target population is drawn from the Business Register and classified by NAICS: 'The target population for the MSM consists of all statistical establishments on the Business Register that are classified to the manufacturing sector (by NAICS), which are categorized into over 156 industries.' Sales for low-revenue establishments are derived from GST files rather than collected, which is an administrative input with no publication behind it.
targetReport.cadence_note: Monthly. Record 2101 states 'Frequency: Monthly'. Two things about the historical record are worth keeping: the MSM was benchmarked to the Annual Survey of Manufacturing and Logging only 'up to and including 2003', so that specific arrangement has not held for two decades, and the present-tense relationship in the other direction is stated by the annual survey's own record rather than by this one.

targetReport.title: National Pensions Act, 1992 (Act No. 10 of 1992)
targetReport.publisher: Government of the Republic of Namibia
targetReport.description: Namibia's foundational statute for the universal old-age pension, read section-by-section this session via NamibLII. VERIFIED DIRECTLY. Purpose: 'to provide for national pensions to be paid to aged, blind and disabled persons' (Social Protection Policy 2021-2030's own citation of the Act, p.15, s.5.3, quoted verbatim: 'The National Pensions Act, 1992 (No. 10 of 1992), provides for national pensions to be paid to aged, visually impaired and persons with disability, and to provide for matters incidental thereto'). On amount-setting, s.16(1)(b) assigns 'the payment of national pensions including the maximum amount to be paid, the determination of the amount to be paid in any particular case' to ministerial regulation; s.16(3) permits 'different pensions to be paid to different categories of aged persons according to their income and other assets'; s.16(2) requires parliamentary approval only for reductions to aggregate pension entitlements. The Minister acts 'in consultation with the Minister of Finance'. No section ties any amount to the Consumer Price Index or any price index -- the mechanism is explicitly ministerial/regulatory discretion, not an absence of a stated mechanism.

targetReport.title: Pension Reform Act, 2014
targetReport.description: Nigeria's framework pension statute. Section 15(4) is quoted directly in PenCom's own December 2025 circular (VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session): 'Section 15(4) of the Pension Reform Act (PRA) 2014 guarantees the right of retirees of the Public Service of the Federation to pension review.' Section 53 is separately invoked, per Grok's round (secondary, via PenCom statements as reported in press coverage, not independently quoted from the Act itself or a primary circular) as the basis for PenCom's enforcement action increasing legacy NSITF pensions -- see ng-nsitf-legacy-pension-enforcement. Neither section prescribes a CPI or inflation-based formula; both require periodic review without specifying the method, leaving quantum and timing to administrative determination -- the same shape as the Constitution's own s.173(3) (quoted in full under ng-pencom-federal-pension-review-circular), which requires review 'every five years or together with any Federal Civil Service salary reviews, whichever is earlier' but not a calculation method.

targetReport.title: European System of Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010)
targetReport.publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
targetReport.description: The EU's national accounts framework, enacted as Regulation (EU) No 549/2013. Article 1(2) sets out its two parts: 'a methodology (Annex A) on common standards, definitions, classifications and accounting rules that shall be used for compiling accounts and tables on comparable bases for the purposes of the Union' and 'a programme (Annex B) setting out the time limits by which Member States shall transmit to the Commission (Eurostat) the accounts and tables'. Unlike the international standards already in this corpus, ESA 2010 is a Regulation — member states do not adopt it by choice — which is why the EU branch was expected to produce supranational-to-national edges the Canada/US pair lacks. Annex B turned out to name tables and deadlines rather than publications; see the _dropped entries here and in eu-draft-budget.json.
targetReport.cadence_note: A generational standard, revised roughly once every fifteen to twenty years: ESA 1995 preceded it, and a further revision is already anticipated. releases_per_year matches sna-2008 (0.05) so the two read at the same pulse rate; see _open_questions.

release_schedule.note: 2030 is Eurostat's stated aim, not a locked legal date — the ESA 2030 proposal is still in consultation.

results.basis: The current 'Benefit Rate Adjustments' policy (last updated July 2, 2026) in the Disability Income Assistance Policy Manual states: 'AISH and ADAP benefit rates are adjusted annually, effective January 1st of each year. Starting January 1, 2026, the rate of adjustment is based on the standard escalator amount established under section 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act.' It adds: 'Annual benefit rate changes are calculated using the standard escalator amount established in the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act, which is the lesser of either two per cent, or the Alberta Consumer Price Index (CPI) amount from October through September year-over-year.' results.basis: Alberta Personal Income Tax Act, RSA 2000 c A-30, s. 44.2(0.1)(b) defines the Alberta escalator, absent a prescribed percentage, as the lesser of 2% and the amount determined by the formula A/B - 1, 'where A is the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for the 12-month period that ended on the last September 30 before that year, and B is the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for the 12-month period immediately preceding'. Section 11 in full: '11(1) In this section, “Alberta CPI” means the monthly All-items Consumer Price Index for Alberta, not seasonally adjusted, published by Statistics Canada. (2) The maximum amount of the accommodation charge set by the Minister under section 9(4) of the Act in respect of each type of accommodation must be adjusted annually on August 1 by the lesser of the following: (a) the percentage increase in the Alberta CPI for the 12-month period ending on February 28 of that year, rounded to the nearest $0.05; (b) 3.8%.' This both settles the edge and explains the number on Alberta Health's programme page: the 1.8% increase stated to take effect August 1, 2026 is the CPI figure under (a), sitting below the 3.8% cap under (b) and so the binding term. Note the reference window is 12 months ending February 28, not September 30 as in the other Alberta-CPI edges in this slice -- this regulation runs its own, differently-dated formula.

targetReport.publisher: National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR)

VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session via the June 2026 edition (published July 2026), cross-checked against the March 2024 and July 2025 editions for stability of wording. 'The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a measure of the average change over time of goods and services purchased by households. The CPI uses a Modified Laspeyres formula to calculate the index.' targetReport.title: Monthly Survey of Manufacturing (MSM)
targetReport.description: Monthly survey of Canadian manufacturing sales, inventories, unfilled orders and capacity utilisation, IMDB record 2101. Named as an indicator source by the monthly GDP-by-industry programme for most manufacturing industries, and named alongside the IPPI in the deflation rows of that programme's source table. The target population is drawn from the Business Register and classified by NAICS: 'The target population for the MSM consists of all statistical establishments on the Business Register that are classified to the manufacturing sector (by NAICS), which are categorized into over 156 industries.' Sales for low-revenue establishments are derived from GST files rather than collected, which is an administrative input with no publication behind it.
targetReport.cadence_note: Monthly. Record 2101 states 'Frequency: Monthly'. Two things about the historical record are worth keeping: the MSM was benchmarked to the Annual Survey of Manufacturing and Logging only 'up to and including 2003', so that specific arrangement has not held for two decades, and the present-tense relationship in the other direction is stated by the annual survey's own record rather than by this one.

release_schedule.rule: Under the FFIEC/FDIC/OCC/Federal Reserve interagency Call Report instructions, banks without foreign offices (FFIEC 041/051 filers) must submit within 30 calendar days after the report (quarter-end) date; banks with foreign offices (FFIEC 031 filers, more than one foreign office) get 35 calendar days. If the calculated due date falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.
release_schedule.note: Call Reports are filed quarterly for report (as-of) dates March 31, June 30, September 30, and December 31. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis's bank-supervision page lists explicit deadlines through Q3 2026 (confirmed: Dec 31 2025 report due Fri Jan 30 2026 -- verified directly against FDIC's own FIL for Q4 2025 -- and Sept 30 2026 report due Fri Oct 30 2026). The Q4 2026 entry (Dec 31, 2026 report) was not yet listed on any source as of Aug 2026 (FDIC/FFIEC typically publish the FIL for a quarter only after that quarter closes), so I computed it myself: 30 days after Dec 31, 2026 is Jan 30, 2027, which falls on a Saturday, so under the standard weekend-rollover rule the deadline would move to Monday, Feb 1, 2027 -- this specific date is my computation (implied), not yet published by the agencies. The Q2 2026 report (June 30, 2026) was already due July 30, 2026, which is in the past relative to 2026-08-11, so it is omitted.

(g) all moneys paid to the council by the Government as contributions, grants, endowment or otherwise, except where such moneys are paid with a condition as to the purpose for which such moneys are paid...' -- establishing government grants as one permitted category of council revenue, though the Act itself states no allocation formula or percentage; the actual subvention/CIP-grant amounts are set by later Ministry of Housing administrative practice (see sz-mohud-annual-report-2024-25). Section 57(1) separately grants own-source fee authority: 'a council may charge fees for any service or facility provided by it or for any licence or permit issued by it.' HOSTING/QUALITY CAVEAT: this PDF is hosted by Gender Links (genderlinks.org.za), a South African NGO, not an Eswatini-government domain -- no official gov.sz/legislation portal copy could be located (the gov.sz 'ACTS' resources page does not list it). It is nonetheless authentic statutory text; its section numbering is independently corroborated by the Ministry of Housing's FY2024/25 report, which separately cites 'Section 115' and 'Section 8' of the same Act. The scanned/OCR'd PDF also has significant digit-garbling errors (e.g. '35.' for '85.', '36.' for '86.', page-footer range markers like 'ss.85-87' confirming the correct numbering despite garbled in-body digits); the quotes above are reproduced in cleaned form.

targetReport.title: Consumer Price Index Manual: Concepts and Methods
targetReport.publisher: IMF, ILO, OECD, Eurostat, UNECE and the World Bank
targetReport.description: The internationally agreed manual of concepts, methods and practice for compiling a consumer price index. Jointly published by six international organisations and managed by the IMF; the 2020 edition updates the 2004 ILO-managed Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice. Country code is CA only because the schema offers no international option — the publisher is a consortium of international agencies.
targetReport.cadence_note: Revised roughly once a generation — editions in 1989, 2004 and 2020. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal so the pulse rate reads as near-static.

release_schedule.note: No release calendar or stated periodicity exists. The Manual has been issued only three times: 1989 (ILO, 'Consumer Price Indices: An ILO Manual'), 2004 ('Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice'), and 2020 ('Consumer Price Index Manual: Concepts and Methods'), each ~15-16 years apart. The IMF's own page for this report is titled 'Update of the Consumer Price Index Manual' and explains the 2020 edition was produced because 'methods and best practices have continued to evolve' since 2004, following requests from the 2014 UNECE-ILO CPI Experts Meeting -- i.e., updates are triggered by inter-agency expert consensus, not a fixed schedule. No next-edition date or working-group timeline is published. This is consistent with the corpus's very low releases_per_year (0.06, i.e. roughly once per 16 years).

results.basis: SSA states the statutory formula outright: 'The Social Security Act specifies a formula for determining each COLA. According to the formula, COLAs are based on increases in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). CPI-Ws are calculated on a monthly basis by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. A COLA effective for December of the current year is equal to the percentage increase (if any) in the CPI-W from the average for the third quarter of the current year to the average for the third quarter of the last year in which a COLA became effective.' The arithmetic is shown in full: the 2.8 percent COLA effective December 2025 is (317.265 - 308.729) / 308.729 x 100, using the July, August and September CPI-W values for 2024 and 2025. Note the index is CPI-W, a subpopulation index for urban wage earners and clerical workers, not the headline CPI-U.

results.basis: The Handbook of Methods is unambiguous that the survey cannot produce population levels by itself: 'Population controls are independent estimates of the population that are used to weight the CPS sample results so that estimates reflect the civilian noninstitutional population ages 16 and older. The Census Bureau develops the CPS population controls, which are based on decennial census population counts, supplemented with birth and death data and estimates of net international migration. The Census Bureau reviews and adjusts the population estimates every year. BLS introduces the Census Bureau's annual population control adjustments into CPS estimates for January.' This is why the January Employment Situation carries a break in the household series each year — the level jumps by whatever the new vintage says, independent of anything that happened in the labour market.

targetReport.title: Population Estimates Program (Vintage Estimates)
targetReport.description: Annual estimates of the resident population for the nation, states and counties, produced between decennial censuses. Each vintage starts from the most recent decennial census count and carries it forward with administrative records on births, deaths and net international migration. Distinct from the decennial census itself: the census is a count, this is a model built on top of the count, and it is the model rather than the count that most federal programmes and surveys actually use year to year.

targetReport.title: Current Population Survey (CPS)
targetReport.publisher: US Census Bureau and US Bureau of Labor Statistics
targetReport.description: The monthly household survey of about 60,000 eligible households, collected by the Census Bureau and estimated by BLS. It is the sole source of the official unemployment rate and of every labour force measure broken down by age, sex, race, education or reason for unemployment. On average one CPS respondent stands for about 2,500 people, so the survey cannot produce a level on its own — it produces a rate, and the level comes from population controls supplied by Census.

results.window: If a family's total income is less than the family's threshold, then that family and every individual in it is considered in poverty. The official poverty thresholds do not vary geographically, but they are updated for inflation using the Consumer Price Index (CPI-U). The official poverty definition uses money income before taxes and does not include capital gains or noncash benefits (such as public housing, Medicaid, and food stamps).

results.basis: NIPA Handbook Chapter 5 lists the CPI among the principal inputs — 'The following are among the principal source data used for the PCE estimates: BEA's Benchmark Input-Output (I-O) Accounts... the Census Bureau's Annual Retail Trade Survey, Service Annual Survey, Quarterly Services Survey, and Monthly Retail Trade Survey; and the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Indexes (CPIs)' — and then explains the mechanism: 'The estimates of quantities purchased, or real spending, for most of the detailed PCE categories are prepared by deflation. In this method, the quantities are calculated by dividing the current-dollar value of the component by an appropriate price index... For most PCE categories, the closest matching price index is a consumer price index or indexes.' Tables 5.A and 5.B name the specific CPI series component by component (CPI for new cars, CPI for used cars and trucks, CPI for food at home, and so on). The Fed's preferred inflation gauge is therefore largely a reweighting of BLS price quotes onto national-accounts expenditure weights.

release_schedule.note: BLS's Consumer Expenditure Surveys annual news release has historically occurred in September of the year following the survey year (Sept 9 2021, Sept 9 2022, Sept 8 2023, Sept 25 2024, per ALFRED/St. Louis Fed release records). The 2024-data annual release broke this pattern: originally scheduled Sept 23 2025, it was rescheduled to Oct 30 2025 and then finally released Dec 19 2025, due to the 2025 federal government lapse in appropriations (shutdown) and a data-validation issue tied to a 2024 questionnaire redesign (see https://www.bls.gov/cex/notices/2025/ce-2024-reschedule.htm and https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cesan_12192025.htm). As of the research date (2026-08-11), BLS has not published a specific date for the next (2025-data) annual release. BLS notices through mid-2026 (e.g. https://www.bls.gov/cex/notices/2026/missing-ce-data-impact.htm, dated July 1 2026) describe ongoing expert-panel work to address CE data missing from Oct-Nov 2025 because of the shutdown, which could push the next release later than the historical September pattern. No official release-calendar page or stated rule for CEX was found on bls.gov/schedule/news_release/, which does not list CEX among its scheduled principal releases.

results.window: For the CPI to be an accurate cost of living measure, the market basket must correspond to what consumers are actually purchasing, and the different categories of items must be weighted to reflect their proportions in consumers' budgets. The CPI uses data from the Consumer Expenditure (CE) survey to determine the weights of the different categories of goods and services in the CPI. The CE survey collects data on the out-of-pocket expenses spent to acquire all consumer products and services.

targetReport.title: Decennial Census of Population and Housing
targetReport.description: The constitutionally mandated ten-yearly count of the US population. Beyond apportionment, it defines the urban areas in which federal statistical programmes sample and supplies the population counts those samples are weighted to.
targetReport.cadence_note: Every ten years. The enum's coarsest bucket is annual, which is off by a factor of ten here — the same failure the Canadian census already exposes, now with a worse ratio.

release_schedule.rule: Apportionment counts transmitted to the President within 9 months of the census date (13 U.S.C. §141(b)); the census date is April 1 of each decennial year.
release_schedule.note: The 2020 count actually slipped to April 2021 due to COVID-19 — treat the Dec 31 statutory deadline as a target, not a guarantee.

The CPI requires
 a geographic sample, which is a set of areas where prices will be collected;
 a survey of consumer expenditures to create and appropriately weight a market basket of goods and services to be priced and to create a sample of outlets in which prices are collected; and

 Using 2010 census population data, we select the urban areas from which data on prices are collected and choose the housing units within each area that are eligible for use in the shelter component of the CPI. The census data also provide information on the number of consumers represented by each area selected as a CPI price collection area.

results.basis: The CES sampling frame 'is built from unemployment insurance (UI) quarterly tax records', and the net birth–death model that fills the gap left by firms too new to sample is derived from 'the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) universe employment series' via an ARIMA projection on ten years of QCEW history. The annual benchmark revises the estimates against QCEW Q1 data. The monthly payroll number is a sample tethered at both ends to a near-universe count.

targetReport.title: Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages
targetReport.description: A near-universe count of employment and wages compiled from state unemployment insurance quarterly tax records, covering nearly all US employers. Not a sample — which is why it serves as the frame and the benchmark for the monthly employment estimates that move markets.

Q3 2026 and Q4 2026 release dates are listed on the publisher's calendar as 'to be determined in 2027' (not yet dated), so are omitted here. Releases run roughly 8-9 months behind the reference quarter due to the underlying UI wage-record collection lag; as of 2026 BLS consolidated the news release and full data update into a single simultaneous publication date (change effective starting with Q4 2024 data, released June 4, 2025).

From the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) universe employment series, each establishment is classified as a continuing, birth, or death unit. The process outlined in step one is applied to the QCEW data.
